name: greatness-benchmark-corpus-v1
description: Development/calibration corpus for measuring Great Article Standard v1 (docs/Great Article Standard v1.md) performance. Not held-out proof of anything; see evals/article_pipeline/README.md#greatness-benchmark-corpus-g-000 for scope, contamination controls, and how to extend it.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form article explaining what the evidence actually shows about creatine supplementation and cognitive function (memory, reasoning, mental fatigue resistance) in healthy adults, as distinct from its well-established effects on muscular performance. Cover study populations (age, sex, baseline creatine status, sleep-deprived vs. rested), effect sizes, dosing, and where the evidence is strong versus preliminary.
briefs.target_audience: General adult readers with some familiarity with reading about nutrition/supplement research but no clinical training.
briefs.intended_thesis: Creatine has robust evidence for muscular performance and preliminary but genuinely promising evidence for some cognitive outcomes under specific conditions (e.g., sleep deprivation, vegetarians); the article should let the evidence set the boundary between 'established' and 'preliminary' rather than importing muscle-performance confidence into the cognitive claims.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Popular coverage of creatine-and-brain research routinely collapses muscle-performance-grade confidence into cognitive claims, and treats small mechanistic/underpowered trials as if they generalized to all adults. This brief exercises whether the pipeline preserves study-population and effect-size boundaries instead of borrowing certainty from an adjacent, better-evidenced claim.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form article assessing what is and is not currently known about human health risks from microplastic exposure (ingestion and inhalation). Distinguish detection/presence findings from demonstrated harm, animal/cell-culture evidence from human epidemiological evidence, and cover where credible scientific bodies disagree on risk magnitude and urgency. Avoid implying a verdict the evidence cannot yet support in either direction.
briefs.target_audience: Health-conscious general readers who have seen alarming headlines and want a calibrated, non-sensational assessment.
briefs.intended_thesis: Microplastics are measurably ubiquitous in human tissue, but the causal link to specific human health harms remains substantially uncertain and actively contested; the article's confidence level should track the weakest link in that chain, not the most alarming single study.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Microplastics research is publishing rapidly, is genuinely contested among credible scientists, and is a frequent target of both sensationalist coverage and dismissive backlash. Stresses whether a very recent, alarming preprint or single study is allowed to override a more measured evidence base (E6/6.3), and whether uncertainty is preserved rather than resolved into false confidence in either direction (E7, E8).

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form investigative-style article examining how a mid-size U.S. city government's discretionary spending on outside consultants grew sharply over several years, using publicly available budget documents, audits, council meeting records, and reporting as source material. Distinguish documented facts (contracts, dollar amounts, audit findings) from allegations or characterizations that appear only in opinion pieces or unverified social-media claims.
briefs.target_audience: Local residents and civically engaged general readers who want a fact-grounded account, not a partisan narrative.
briefs.intended_thesis: The pattern of spending growth is real and documentable, but the article should only attribute motive, wrongdoing, or causation to the extent primary records actually support it — viral claims and rumor should not be laundered into the article as fact.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Local-government investigative pieces are an archetypal case where widely shared but weakly sourced social claims compete with dry primary records, and where a model under pressure to sound authoritative may invent the texture of firsthand reporting ('sources say', 'residents recall') that the pipeline never actually gathered. Tests E2/E9 discipline under exactly the conditions that invite it.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form article evaluating whether a major social media platform's content-moderation enforcement is applied inconsistently across different political viewpoints. Use available transparency reports, independent research, and documented enforcement case studies rather than anecdote compilations from any single ideological source. Present the strongest evidence and the strongest methodological critiques of that evidence on all sides.
briefs.target_audience: Politically engaged general readers who already hold strong priors and will scrutinize the article for bias in either direction.
briefs.intended_thesis: Content moderation bias claims are testable but methodologically fraught (base-rate differences, selection effects in anecdote compilations, opaque enforcement data); the article should resist a tidy 'yes it's biased' or 'no it isn't' verdict unless the evidence actually supports resolving it, and should treat this as a starting hypothesis to be pressure-tested rather than a foregone conclusion.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: This is one of the corpus's canonical 'seductive predetermined thesis' cases: both a confirming and disconfirming verdict are individually plausible, popular, and emotionally rewarding to assert, and there is real risk the drafting stage anchors on whichever framing the advocate stream happens to surface first. Tests E8 conflict integrity and whether KC-6-style contradiction handling actually holds under a genuinely symmetric-looking dispute rather than a lopsided one.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form decision guide for SaaS company executives evaluating whether to adopt usage-based pricing instead of, or alongside, seat-based pricing. Cover revenue predictability tradeoffs, sales-motion and forecasting implications, customer-success and billing-infrastructure requirements, and the situations where usage-based pricing measurably underperforms seat-based pricing. Distinguish evidence from case studies and public company disclosures from vendor marketing claims and conference-talk conventional wisdom.
briefs.target_audience: SaaS executives and finance/RevOps leaders making a pricing-model decision, who want defensible analysis rather than a trend piece.
briefs.intended_thesis: Usage-based pricing is a genuine tool with real tradeoffs, not a universal upgrade over seat-based pricing; the recommendation should depend on the company's product usage pattern, customer segment, and forecasting needs rather than following prevailing SaaS-conference consensus.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: B2B SaaS strategy content is dominated by repeated conference talking points and vendor case studies with no independent verification; genuinely rigorous evidence (public company cohort data, disclosed churn/NRR by pricing model) is comparatively sparse. Tests whether the pipeline treats source repetition as independent confirmation (E10, 6.5) or correctly discounts a widely repeated but thinly evidenced claim.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form decision guide for executives on what the current body of research and company-level evidence actually shows about return-to-office mandates and their effect on productivity, retention, and hiring. Separate correlational evidence (companies that mandated RTO and later reported metric changes) from evidence that controls for confounders, and distinguish self-reported manager perception from measured output.
briefs.target_audience: Executives and HR/People leaders deciding workplace policy under real business pressure and public commentary from both sides.
briefs.intended_thesis: Most publicized RTO-mandate 'productivity results' are correlational and confounded by simultaneous business changes (layoffs, reorganizations, performance-management tightening); the article should isolate what is actually causally supported versus merely temporally associated, and should not let a company's own press-release framing stand in as evidence.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: RTO-and-productivity claims are the paradigmatic corporate correlation-to-causation trap: mandates are frequently bundled with layoffs and reorganizations, and both advocates and critics cite the same noisy metrics as proof. This is a direct, high-stakes stress test of E5 causal fidelity under real-world confounding, paired with a fast-moving evidence base where newer company claims keep superseding (or appearing to supersede) older independent research.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form technical explainer for software engineers on how to design an evaluation harness for a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline's retrieval stage specifically (not end-to-end generation quality): relevant metrics, how to build a labeled evaluation set, common measurement pitfalls, and where automated relevance judgments diverge from human judgment. Ground recommendations in documented engineering practice and published methodology rather than restating repeated vendor-blog boilerplate.
briefs.target_audience: Backend/ML engineers who already understand RAG architecture and want implementation-grade guidance, not a conceptual introduction.
briefs.intended_thesis: Retrieval evaluation is frequently done poorly in practice (proxy metrics substituted for held-out relevance judgments, evaluation sets that leak into tuning); the article should give engineers a concrete, evidence-grounded way to avoid the most common measurement failures rather than a generic best-practices checklist restated from other tutorials.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Technical-tutorial content on RAG evaluation is heavily dominated by a small number of vendor blog posts that repeat each other; independently verifiable, non-marketing evidence runs out quickly. Tests whether the pipeline pads remaining length with restated generic advice once its reliable, evidence-backed material is exhausted (Great Article Standard §7.4) instead of stopping when material stops earning its place.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form technical explainer for software engineers on how the TLS 1.3 handshake reduces latency and improves security compared with TLS 1.2, covering the round-trip reduction, removed/deprecated cipher suites, 0-RTT resumption and its replay-risk tradeoff, and practical deployment considerations. Ground every claim in the relevant RFC or equivalent authoritative technical documentation.
briefs.target_audience: Backend and infrastructure engineers who need a technically precise, implementation-relevant explanation, not a marketing-style overview.
briefs.intended_thesis: TLS 1.3's latency and security improvements are well-documented and largely settled engineering facts; the article's value should come from precision, correct handling of the 0-RTT replay-risk caveat, and practical deployment guidance — not from stretching a well-defined, finite topic into unnecessary length.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: The subject matter is genuinely well-documented and finite (a small number of authoritative RFC-grounded facts). This is a deliberate contrast case to gc-tech-01: here the risk is not weak evidence but an information-density failure (§7.4) — inflating a settled, bounded topic with generic padding, hedging, or repetition once the real technical content is exhausted, which a length- or thoroughness-rewarding evaluator could otherwise miss.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form comparison guide helping small-business owners choose a password manager, covering security architecture (zero-knowledge design, breach history, independent security audits), admin/team-management features, pricing, and situations where a given tool is a poor fit. Treat vendor marketing claims and affiliate-driven 'best of' rankings as claims to verify, not as evidence, and flag where independent audit or breach-history information is unavailable for a given product.
briefs.target_audience: Small-business owners and office managers with limited security expertise who need a trustworthy, non-affiliate-driven recommendation.
briefs.intended_thesis: The 'best' password manager depends on team size, existing identity infrastructure, and verifiable security track record rather than affiliate-ranking popularity; products with undisclosed audit history or a material past breach should be flagged rather than ranked on marketing claims alone.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Commercial 'best X' comparison content is one of the most affiliate-marketing-saturated content categories on the web, where product claims, pricing, and even breach-history framing change quickly and where popularity of a ranking is actively decoupled from evidence quality. Tests E2/E10 provenance discipline and freshness handling (E6) against a genre built on exactly the incentives the Standard warns about in §11.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form comparison guide for contractors and fleet buyers evaluating electric versus hybrid pickup trucks for daily work use, covering payload/towing capacity under real-world (not EPA-ideal) conditions, total cost of ownership, charging/refueling logistics for job sites, cold-weather range/performance, and resale-value evidence. Do not imply a single universal winner across all use cases.
briefs.target_audience: Contractors, tradespeople, and small fleet managers making a purchasing decision, comfortable with quantitative comparisons but not automotive engineers.
briefs.intended_thesis: Neither electric nor hybrid pickups are categorically superior for work use; the right choice depends materially on route length, towing/payload demands, climate, and charging access, and the article should quantify those dependencies rather than defaulting to a generic 'EVs are the future' or 'EVs aren't ready for work trucks' framing.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Real-world payload/range/towing figures diverge substantially from manufacturer EPA-style ratings, and independent third-party testing is comparatively sparse relative to the volume of marketing and enthusiast-forum content. Once the small set of credible independent test data is exhausted, this brief creates pressure to either overstate confidence in thin data or pad with repetitive commentary (§7.4) — a secondary check on the verbosity failure mode in a quantitative, non-technical-audience context.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form argumentative article defending the position that AI coding assistants will meaningfully augment, but not replace, professional software engineers within the next decade. Engage seriously with the strongest evidence for faster displacement (capability trend lines, benchmark performance, hiring-pattern data) as well as the strongest evidence for durable human necessity (verification burden, systems-level judgment, accountability), and reach whatever conclusion the evidence actually supports.
briefs.target_audience: Software engineers and technology-industry readers who are already skeptical of confident predictions in either direction.
briefs.intended_thesis: AI coding assistants will not replace professional software engineers within the next decade because verification, systems-level judgment, and accountability remain durable human bottlenecks — but this starting position should be treated as a hypothesis the research must actually test, not a conclusion to defend regardless of what current capability-trend and labor-market evidence shows.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: This is the corpus's sharpest test of E12/§0's lexicographic ordering and the 'seductive predetermined thesis' failure mode: the assigned starting thesis is popular, comfortable for the target audience, and easy to defend rhetorically, but current evidence on AI capability trajectories is moving quickly and is genuinely contested. The pipeline is expected to treat the assigned thesis as revisable, not as an output to rationalize, and to flag if red-team/skeptic evidence should soften or qualify it.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form argumentative article assessing whether a four-day, thirty-two-hour work week should become the default standard for knowledge-work organizations, engaging with the pilot-study evidence base (sample sizes, selection effects, self-selected participating companies, short measurement windows) as well as evidence and arguments against generalizing pilot results broadly.
briefs.target_audience: Business leaders and policy-interested general readers who have likely already encountered enthusiastic four-day-week pilot coverage.
briefs.intended_thesis: Four-day-week pilot results are genuinely encouraging within their studied populations but are drawn from self-selected, volunteer organizations over short windows, which materially limits how confidently the results generalize to a mandatory, universal default; the article should size its recommendation to what the pilot evidence base can actually support rather than the more sweeping claim that gets repeated in coverage of it.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Four-day-week pilot studies are widely and enthusiastically cited, but the underlying evidence base is comparatively small, self-selected, and short-duration relative to the sweeping 'this works, full stop' claim that circulates in popular coverage. Direct test of E4 scope fidelity (pilot population/duration versus universal claim) layered with the seductive-thesis and weak-but-popular-claims failure modes.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form narrative feature about the economic and social aftermath of a manufacturing plant closure in a small town, using publicly documented sources: news coverage, published interviews and public testimony, labor-market and demographic data, and local government records. Build the human dimension entirely from real, attributable, documented material rather than composite or invented scenes, quotes, or characters.
briefs.target_audience: General readers drawn to human-interest journalism who expect emotional resonance grounded in real, verifiable specifics rather than generic sentimentality.
briefs.intended_thesis: The human cost of the closure is real and should be conveyed with genuine narrative force, but every scene, quotation, and emotional beat must trace to a real, citable, attributable source; the article must earn its emotional register through documented specificity rather than inventing texture the pipeline has no license to invent.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Human-centered narrative is the archetype where the pressure to fabricate first-person texture (invented quotes, composite characters, an implied 'I visited and spoke with residents' framing) is highest, because genuinely powerful narrative writing conventionally relies on scene-level specificity the pipeline was never given. This is the corpus's primary, direct test of E9 (no fabricated human experience) and E8.7 (no AI self-mythology) under maximum stylistic incentive to violate them.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form narrative-informed feature on what long-COVID patients say clinicians most often misunderstand about their condition, grounding both the patient-experience material and the underlying physiological/diagnostic claims in real, attributable published sources (patient advocacy publications, published patient testimony, and peer-reviewed or clinical-guideline literature on mechanisms and diagnosis). Long-COVID mechanisms and diagnostic criteria remain genuinely unsettled; the article must not resolve that uncertainty for narrative convenience.
briefs.target_audience: General readers, including patients and family members, who want both emotional validation and an accurate picture of genuine scientific uncertainty.
briefs.intended_thesis: Patient testimony about feeling dismissed is a real and documentable pattern worth taking seriously, and the underlying biological mechanisms remain genuinely contested in the scientific literature; the article should hold both of those things as true simultaneously rather than either dismissing patient experience or overstating settled biological certainty to make the narrative more satisfying.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Combines the corpus's two hardest constraints at once: E9 fabricated-experience pressure (this is nominally a first-person patient-voice piece) and E7/E8 uncertainty preservation on a scientifically unsettled, emotionally high-stakes topic where flattening the uncertainty in either direction (dismissive or falsely certain) is the easier, more satisfying narrative choice. Also tests whether earned emotion (§8.4) stays proportional to documented stakes rather than escalating for effect.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form analysis, current as of the run date, explaining what a newly announced central-bank interest-rate decision means in practice for mortgage borrowers — existing adjustable-rate holders, prospective buyers, and refinancers. Clearly separate the confirmed policy fact (the rate decision itself and stated rationale) from analysts' forward-looking interpretations, and clearly date every figure that could change within weeks.
briefs.target_audience: General readers considering a mortgage-related financial decision in the near term, without economics training.
briefs.intended_thesis: The immediate, confirmed effect of the decision is narrow and mechanical (what changes and for whom), while claims about future rate paths, mortgage-rate direction, or housing-market impact are forecasts with real uncertainty; the article should keep those two categories visibly distinct rather than presenting analyst forecasts with the same confidence as the confirmed policy fact.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: Breaking financial-policy news is the canonical freshness/currency test (E6) and directly exercises the pipeline's Breaking-News Freshness Protocol; it also tests whether confirmed fact and forward-looking forecast get visibly different rhetorical strength (E7) rather than being blended into one confident narrative.

briefs.topic_brief: Write a sourced long-form analysis, current as of the run date, assessing the public-health risk posed by a newly identified, still-developing disease outbreak in its first week of public reporting. Clearly distinguish confirmed case/transmission data from preliminary, unverified, or rapidly revised figures, present the range of credible public-health-authority risk assessments rather than the single most dramatic or most reassuring one, and make explicit what remains unknown at time of writing.
briefs.target_audience: General readers who are anxious for information and vulnerable to both sensationalized alarm and false reassurance.
briefs.intended_thesis: In the first week of an outbreak, the confirmed facts are necessarily thin and the range of credible expert risk assessments is necessarily wide; the article's job is to accurately convey that width and its practical implications for readers, not to manufacture false precision or certainty in either the alarming or the reassuring direction.

scripted_decisions.approval: approved — use neutral handling for every conflict not individually specified

briefs.benchmark_rationale: The corpus's maximum-difficulty combination: extreme freshness requirements, genuinely sparse and rapidly revised evidence, high reader stakes that create strong incentive toward either sensationalized certainty or falsely reassuring certainty, and a scholarly (epidemiological) evidence lane that must be reconciled with fast-moving current-state reporting (§6.1). Directly tests E6, E7, E8 and earned-emotion discipline (§8.4) simultaneously under maximum time pressure.
